title: Describing people
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE LONG ADJECTIVE ARRIVES, and L1 set it up without saying so. ustál, ustála and ustáli (L1-M2) are SHORT-form adjectives, which can only stand where English puts them after "is"; rússkiy (L1-M1) is a long one. This module teaches the long form and its four nominative endings — vysókiy · vysókaya · vysókoye · vysókiye — which stand both in front of a noun and after the missing "is". The short form is not a shortening of the long one, and only a handful of adjectives use it in everyday speech: ustál, svobóden, zányat, rad.

There is still NO COPULA. On vysókiy is two words and complete, exactly as L1-M1's Ya studént was. The adjective's ending does all the work the English "is" would have done, which is why choosing it correctly matters more here than in any module so far.

yevó and yeyó each carry TWO jobs: "his" and "him", "her" and "her". Russian's genitive and accusative pronouns are also its possessives, so one word covers what English splits. After a preposition they take an n-, which is why u nevó and u neyó look different from yevó and yeyó — same words, one spelling rule.

POSSESSION EXTENDS L1-M8's FRAME to other people: U nevó yest' brat is literally "at him there is a brother". That is the same oblique-person habit as M1's Mne núzhno — the person is not the subject. Yevó zovút Iván extends L1-M1's Menyá zovút the same way: the pattern is already the learner's, and only the pronoun is new.

Two words in this module's family set are irregular and are taught as words rather than as examples of anything. mat' and doch' are feminine nouns ending in a consonant plus a soft sign, and they decline unlike anything else in the course — their shapes are in their rows and no rule claims they are regular. And vesyólyy carries a yó, which must be written: one word, one spelling.

words.note: The four nominative shapes of a long adjective: masculine, feminine, neuter, plural. One row holds the whole paradigm, and M3 will add its case shapes here rather than open a second row.
Masculine, and regular. The shapes here are the ones the level shows: subject, object or possessed, recipient.
The masculine "my". It agrees with what is owned, never with the owner — moy brat whoever is speaking.

sentences.trap: There is no word for "is" and none is missing. Two words are the whole sentence, and the -iy ending is what tells you the sentence is about a masculine person.
sentences.sound: moy brat vy-SO-kiy. The y of vysókiy is the hard back vowel, made with the tongue pulled back — not the ee of English "see".

variations.changed: feminine throughout — both the possessive and the adjective move
a pronoun instead of a named person
negated with ne in front of the adjective

mistake.why: sestrá is feminine, so both words move with it: Moyá sestrá vysókaya.

sentences.usage: Describing family — the first thing anyone is asked about.
sentences.mnemonic: The endings follow the noun, not the speaker.

words.note: A long adjective whose stress sits on the ending, so every shape keeps the mark on the last syllable. That is a real pattern, not an accident of this word.
Feminine and regular. Stress on the ending here too, which is why the first e reduces almost to i in speech.
The feminine "my", and its own row rather than a cell of moy's — the L1 policy keeps a form a learner must choose between on a row of its own.

sentences.trap: Both endings are stressed, which is unusual and audible. molodáya is ma-la-DA-ya, and the two unstressed o's reduce to a — the spelling is the only place they survive.
sentences.sound: ma-YA sist-RA ma-la-DA-ya. Four unstressed vowels reduce in a row, which is what makes Russian sound faster than it is.

variations.changed: masculine throughout
a pronoun instead of a named person
óchen' added in front of the adjective

mistake.why: The adjective agrees with sestrá: Moyá sestrá molodáya.

sentences.usage: Describing family, and the shape every answer about age starts from.
sentences.mnemonic: Where the stress falls, it stays.

words.note: One word, two jobs: the object "him" and the possessive "his". After a preposition it becomes nevó, which is the same word wearing a spelling rule.
The feminine twin, and it too covers both jobs. The yó must be written — one word, one spelling.

sentences.trap: The spelling lies about the sound: его is said yi-VO, with a v where the letter г stands. That is a rule of the language rather than an exception, and it holds in every genitive ending in -ого.
sentences.sound: yi-VO za-VUT i-VAN. The stress is on the last syllable of yevó, and the g is a v.

variations.changed: the feminine pronoun
back to L1-M1's version — the same frame, a different person
the question, with kak rather than chto

mistake.why: The frame takes the object form: Yevó zovút Iván.

sentences.usage: Introducing someone who is not present, or asking about them.
sentences.mnemonic: Nobody has a name in Russian — they call you one.

words.note: yevó with an n- in front, which every preposition puts there. It rides as a whole surface beside L1-M8's u menyá, and the n- is a spelling rule with nothing to work out.
The same rule on yeyó. u neyó, never u yeyó — and the yó is written here too.

sentences.trap: This is L1-M8's u menyá yest' with a different person in it, not a new idiom. The owner is never the subject in Russian: the thing owned is.
sentences.sound: u nyi-VO yest' brat. Same v-for-g as in yevó, and yest' ends soft.

variations.changed: the feminine pronoun and a different relative
a thing rather than a person
the negative, which puts the thing in the genitive

mistake.why: A preposition puts an n- in front: U nevó yest' brat.

sentences.usage: Talking about someone else's family, car, job or trouble.
sentences.mnemonic: A preposition adds an n. Every time.

words.note: The e disappears whenever an ending is added — otéts but ottsá. That vanishing vowel is common in Russian masculines and is worth expecting.
Feminine, ending in a consonant plus a soft sign, and irregular: an -er- appears in every shape but this one. Learn it as a word, not as an example.

sentences.trap: Éhto does not agree with anything. It is a flat pointing word, so Éhto moy otéts and Éhto moyá mat' both start the same way — only what follows moves.
sentences.sound: EH-ta moy a-TYETS. The final o of éhto reduces to a, and the ts of otéts is one sound, not two.

variations.changed: feminine, and an irregular noun
a different masculine relative
negated, with ne before what it denies

mistake.why: The pointing word does not agree here: Éhto moyá mat'.

sentences.usage: Handing round a photograph, or introducing someone at a door.
sentences.mnemonic: Éhto never moves. Everything after it does.

sentences.display: Éhto moy syn i moyá doch'
sentences.script: Это мой сын и моя дочь
sentences.cue: This is my son and my daughter
sentences.literal: This my son and my daughter

words.note: Masculine, with an irregular plural in -ovyá. The singular shapes are ordinary.
mat's twin in every way: feminine, consonant plus soft sign, and an -er- appearing in every shape but this one. The two are learnt together.
The neuter "my", for words like pis'mó and útro. Written with the yó, and stressed on the ending.
The plural "my", for more than one of anything, whatever their gender: moí knígi, moí druz'yá.

sentences.trap: mat' and doch' are the only two nouns of this shape in the course, and they behave the same way. Meeting them as a pair is the cheapest way to keep them.
sentences.sound: EH-ta moy syn i ma-YA doch. Both syn and doch' are one syllable, so neither takes a stress mark.

variations.changed: one person instead of two
a neuter noun, so the neuter possessive
plural, and one possessive covers every gender

mistake.why: doch' is feminine despite ending in a consonant: Éhto moyá doch'.

sentences.usage: Introducing children, or naming who is in a photograph.
sentences.mnemonic: A soft sign after a consonant on a person: feminine, and irregular.

words.note: Feminine and regular, with the stress on the ending. The zh is the sound in the middle of English "measure".
Masculine, one syllable, so no stress mark. It also means "man" in older and formal Russian, which is where the word comes from.

sentences.trap: zh is always hard in Russian, whatever vowel follows. zhená sounds zhy-NA and not zhi-NA, which is why the spelling with e is no guide to the sound.
sentences.sound: EH-ta ma-YA zhy-NA. Three unstressed vowels, all reduced, and the stress lands only at the end.

variations.changed: masculine throughout
a statement of where rather than who
negated

mistake.why: zhená is feminine: Éhto moyá zhená.

sentences.usage: Introducing a partner, which in Russian is done with these two words and no others.
sentences.mnemonic: zh is always hard, whatever vowel follows.

words.note: A male friend, or a friend of unspecified sex. The plural is irregular — druz'yá — and the g softens to z' in it.
A female friend. Russian splits what English keeps as one word, so the sex of a friend is unavoidable rather than optional.
The long form of the word L1-M10 met inside dóbryy den' and dóbroye útro. Now it is a describing word in its own right, with its own paradigm.

sentences.trap: M1's bud'te dobrý used the SHORT form of this word, with the stress on the ending. dóbryy is the long form, stressed on the stem. Same adjective, two shapes, two stresses.
sentences.sound: moy druk O-chin' DO-bryy. A final g goes voiceless and comes out as k, which is why drug ends in a k sound.

variations.changed: a female friend, and everything moves with her

variations.cue: My friend is kind and clever
variations.changed: two adjectives joined with i
a pronoun instead of a named person

mistake.why: A female friend is podrúga: Moyá podrúga óchen' dóbraya.

sentences.usage: Talking about the people around you — and the word chosen already says their sex.
sentences.mnemonic: drug for him, podrúga for her. No neutral option.

words.note: Stressed on the stem, so every shape keeps the mark in the same place. It is a warm word, closer to "bright" than to "clever".
The yó is written in every shape, because the yó rule is about one word having one spelling. The stress always sits on it — a yó is never unstressed.

sentences.trap: A yó carries the stress by definition. So a word with one needs no other mark, and a word written with e where a yó belongs is telling the reader the wrong syllable.
sentences.sound: a-NA UM-na-ya i vi-SYO-la-ya. The yó is the yo of English "yonder", and it is where the beat falls.

variations.changed: masculine, so both adjectives move
a named person and one adjective
one adjective only

mistake.why: Both adjectives follow oná: Oná úmnaya i vesyólaya.

sentences.usage: Character rather than looks — and these two are the compliments people actually pay.
sentences.mnemonic: A yó is always stressed, so it never needs a mark of its own.

sentences.cue: My father is old, but good

words.note: Used of people and of things alike. Of a person it is blunter than English "old" and is usually softened or avoided to someone's face.
The adjective behind L1-M2's khoroshó. The neuter ending is -eye rather than -oye, because sh cannot be followed by o here — a spelling rule, not a different word.

sentences.trap: khoróshiy's neuter is khorósheye and not khoróshoye. After the hushing consonants, an unstressed o is written e — the same rule that makes so many adjective tables look irregular when they are not.
sentences.sound: moy a-TYETS STA-ryy no kha-RO-shiy. The kh is the sound at the end of Scottish "loch", made further back than an English h.

variations.changed: the first half alone
in front of a noun rather than after the missing "is"

variations.cue: She is old, but very cheerful
variations.changed: feminine, with óchen' on the second adjective

mistake.why: Both adjectives describe otéts: Moy otéts stáryy, no khoróshiy.

sentences.usage: A real description, with a but in it — which is how people actually talk about their families.
sentences.mnemonic: Long adjectives stand both in front of a noun and alone after it.
